topics.title: 1.1 How can weather be hazardous?

outcomes.text: Outline the global circulation system and how high and low pressure belts create climatic zones.
Explain how global atmospheric circulation causes extreme weather in different parts of the world.
Compare extremes of wind, temperature and precipitation in contrasting countries.
Describe the distribution and frequency of tropical storms and drought and whether they have changed over time.
Outline the causes of extreme weather linked to tropical storms.
Outline how El Nino and La Nina cause drought.
Study two contrasting weather hazard events (one UK, one not; flash flood or tropical storm, and heat wave or drought).
For each chosen event, explain the place-specific causes, consequences and responses.

topics.title: 1.2 How do plate tectonics shape our world?

outcomes.text: Describe the structure of the Earth.
Explain how slab pull and ridge push move tectonic plates.
Describe the processes at constructive, destructive, conservative and collision boundaries and at hotspots.
Explain how plate movement causes shallow and deep focus earthquakes and shield and composite volcanoes.
Study one hazardous tectonic event: its specific causes, consequences and responses.
Explain how technology (building design, prediction, early warning) helps mitigate a tectonic hazard in a chosen area.

topics.title: 2.1 What evidence is there to suggest climate change is a natural process?

outcomes.text: Describe the pattern of climate change from the start of the Quaternary to today.
Judge the range and reliability of climate evidence such as sea ice, ice cores, temperature data, paintings and diaries.
Outline natural causes of climate change: sunspots, volcanic eruptions and Milankovitch cycles.
Explain the natural greenhouse effect and how humans enhance it.
Explore social, economic and environmental impacts of climate change worldwide, such as sea level rise and extreme weather.
Explore social, economic and environmental impacts of climate change within the UK this century.

topics.title: 3.1 What makes a landscape distinctive?

outcomes.text: Define landscape and tell built from natural landscapes.
Describe the distribution of upland, lowland and glaciated landscapes in the UK.
Describe what makes these landscapes distinctive: geology, climate and human activity.

topics.title: 3.2 What influences the landscapes of the UK?

outcomes.text: Explain weathering, mass movement, erosion, transport and deposition.
Explain how headlands, bays, caves, arches, stacks, beaches and spits form.
Explain how waterfalls, gorges, V-shaped valleys, floodplains, levees, meanders and ox-bow lakes form.
Study a UK coastal landscape and a river basin: landforms made by geomorphic processes.
Explain how geology and climate influence processes at different scales in the chosen landscapes.
Explain how human activity and management combine with geomorphic processes to affect the landscape.

topics.title: 4.1 Why are natural ecosystems important?

outcomes.text: Explain an ecosystem as the interdependence of climate, soil, water, plants and animals.
Outline the global distribution of polar regions, coral reefs, grasslands, temperate forests, tropical forests and hot deserts.
Give an overview of the climate, plants and animals of these ecosystems.

topics.title: 4.2 Why should tropical rainforests matter to us?

outcomes.text: Describe rainforest characteristics: climate, nutrient cycle, soil profile and water cycle.
Explain the interdependence of climate, soil, water, plants, animals and people in rainforests.
Explore the value of rainforests through their goods and services.
Describe human impacts from logging, mining, agriculture and tourism.
Study a case of sustainable rainforest management such as ecotourism, community programmes, reserves or sustainable forestry.

topics.title: 4.3 Is there more to polar environments than ice?

outcomes.text: Outline the climate, land, sea, plants and animals of Antarctica and the Arctic.
Explain the interdependence of climate, soil, water, plants, animals and people in the Antarctic or the Arctic.
Explore human impacts on polar ecosystems such as research, indigenous people, tourism, fishing, whaling and mining.
Study one small-scale example of sustainable management in a polar region.
Study one global example of sustainable polar management, such as Earth Summits or the Antarctic Treaty.

topics.title: 5.1 Why do more than half the world's population live in urban areas?

outcomes.text: Explain how urban growth rates vary between places at different levels of development.
Outline features of world cities and megacities and how their distribution changed since 1950.
Explain causes of rapid urbanisation in LIDCs, including push and pull factors and natural growth.
Investigate consequences of rapid urban growth in LIDCs.
Explain causes and consequences of suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation in ACs.

topics.title: 5.2 What are the challenges and opportunities for cities today?

outcomes.text: Describe the city's location and its importance in its region, country and world.
Explain how national and international migration changes the city's growth and character.
Explore ways of life in the city: culture, ethnicity, housing, leisure and consumption.
Investigate current challenges in an AC city, such as housing, transport, services and inequality.
Investigate current challenges in an LIDC or EDC city, such as informal settlements, jobs, health and waste.
Investigate one sustainability initiative in each city, such as brownfield use, recycling or transport.

topics.title: 6.1 Why are some countries richer than others?

outcomes.text: Define development and how countries are classed as AC, EDC or LIDC.
Describe the global distribution of ACs, EDCs and LIDCs.
Use economic and social measures such as GNI per capita and HDI to show uneven development.
Outline human and physical factors behind uneven development.
Explore what keeps countries in poverty: debt, trade and political unrest.

topics.title: 6.2 Are LIDCs likely to stay poor?

outcomes.text: Give an overview of one LIDC's economic development and the roles of population, society, technology and politics.
Explore whether Rostow's model fits the country's path.
Assess progress towards three relevant Sustainable Development Goals.
Investigate how political, social and environmental context affected development.
Explain the effects of trade reliance on one or few commodities.
Explain benefits and problems of trade and TNC investment for development.
Explain advantages and disadvantages of international aid, such as debt relief.
Compare one top-down and one bottom-up development strategy in the country.

topics.title: 7.1 How is the UK changing in the 21st century?

outcomes.text: Give an overview of UK human and physical features such as population density, land use, rainfall and relief.
Explain issues linked to these, including water stress and housing shortages.
Use population pyramids and migration data since 2001 to place the UK on the Demographic Transition Model.
Explain causes, effects, spread of and responses to an ageing population.
Summarise how population structure and ethnic diversity changed in a named UK place since 2001.
Identify major UK economic changes since 2001: jobs, political priorities, employment sectors and working hours.
Investigate the pattern of core UK economic hubs.
Identify changes in one economic hub and its importance to its region and the UK.

topics.title: 7.2 Is the UK losing its global significance?

outcomes.text: Examine the UK's political role in one global conflict through international organisations.
Explore UK media exports, such as television and film, and their global influence.
Explain how ethnic groups contribute to UK cultural life through food, media or fashion.

topics.title: 8.1 Will we run out of natural resources?

outcomes.text: Outline factors making demand outstrip supply of food, energy and water.
Explain how humans modify environments for resources: farming and fishing mechanisation, deforestation and mining, reservoirs and water transfers.

topics.title: 8.2 Can we feed nine billion people by 2050?

outcomes.text: Explain food security and the human and physical factors that influence it.
Describe world patterns of food access, such as the Global Hunger Index and daily calories.
Compare Malthusian and Boserupian theories of population and food supply.
Study one country's food security, using food consumption and availability statistics over time.
Assess one local-scale attempt such as food banks, urban gardens or allotments.
Assess one past and one present national attempt such as food trade, GM crops or the Green Revolution.
Evaluate sustainability of ethical consumerism such as fair trade and reducing food waste.
Evaluate sustainability of food production methods such as organic and intensive farming.
Evaluate sustainability of technology such as GM crops and hydroponics.
Evaluate sustainability of small-scale bottom-up approaches such as urban gardens and permaculture.

topics.title: 9.1 Cartographic skills

outcomes.text: Select and construct maps with suitable scales and annotations.
Interpret cross sections and transects.
Use coordinates, scale and distance.
Extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate map information.
Use gradient, contour and spot heights on OS and other isoline maps.
Describe, interpret and analyse geo-spatial data in a GIS.
Use atlas, OS (1:50 000 and 1:25 000), base, choropleth, isoline, flow line, desire-line, sphere of influence, thematic, route and sketch maps.

topics.title: 9.2 Graphical skills

outcomes.text: Select and construct suitable graphs and charts with appropriate scales and annotations.
Present and communicate data effectively through graphs and charts.
Extract, interpret, analyse and evaluate graph information.

Use bar graphs, histograms, line and scatter graphs, dispersion graphs, pie charts, climate graphs, proportional symbols, pictograms, cross-sections, population pyramids, radial graphs and rose charts.

topics.title: 9.3 Numerical and statistical skills

outcomes.text: Understand number, area and scale.
Understand quantitative relationships between units.
Use proportion, ratio, magnitude and frequency correctly.
Use median, mean, range, quartiles, inter-quartile range, mode, modal class and cumulative frequency.
Calculate percentages (increase and decrease) and percentiles.
Design fieldwork data sheets and collect data with attention to accuracy, sample size, procedures, control groups and reliability.
Interpret tables of data.
Describe relationships in bivariate data.
Sketch trend lines through scatter plots and draw estimated lines of best fit.
Make predictions by interpolating and extrapolating trends.
Identify weaknesses in statistical presentations of data.
Draw and justify conclusions from numerical and statistical data.

topics.title: 9.4 Formulating enquiry and argument

outcomes.text: Deconstruct, interpret, analyse and evaluate visual images such as photographs, cartoons and diagrams.
Analyse written articles for understanding, interpretation and recognising bias.
Suggest improvements, issues with or reasons for using maps, graphs, statistical techniques and visual sources.

topics.title: Fieldwork skills

outcomes.text: Understand the kinds of question fieldwork can investigate and the enquiry process used.
Understand fieldwork techniques and methods, including observation and measurement.
Process and present fieldwork data in maps, graphs and diagrams.
Analyse and explain field data using relevant case studies and theories.
Draw evidenced conclusions and summaries from fieldwork data.
Reflect critically on fieldwork data, methods, conclusions and knowledge gained.
